synopsis: Normal loading, stockpiling, dump-berm approaches and authorized ground-crew proximity can look dangerous to sensors; the booklet identifies wheel loaders as the clearest and hardest case for avoiding nuisance braking [f124, f3022, f11395]. A nuisance warning detects a real object without collision risk, unlike a false warning with no object present; in the NIOSH Caterpillar 793B study, 243 of 478 technically true alarms were nuisance alarms, accounting for 42% of all alarms, demonstrating the need for context rather than sensor precision alone [f5434, f3276, f3279]. Protection must distinguish intended approaches from intruding people or vehicles without simply ignoring loading zones, and legitimate ground-crew proximity requires a controlled task-and-mode concept [f11521, f11863, f3367]. Fixed stop gaps can prevent truck loading, Komatsu requires its stop function to be off during trailer loading, and Volvo uses slope memory to permit reversing down stockpiles; unnecessary automatic stops can themselves be hazardous [f3344, f1538, f10631, f7457]. Validation should use separate production-task scenarios, per-task metrics and shadow-mode reviews before brake actuation, rather than copying road-practice thresholds [f11874, f11876, f10729, f6196]. Evidence gaps remain for stockpile/wall nuisance-alarm frequency and intentional loading/spotting accident rates, while berm terminology is in tension: some facts classify berms as nuisance-warning objects, but another says their protective edge-reference detections should not be treated as nuisance [f3360, f3568, f5434, f11864].

Intended loading approaches are nuisance cases unless another vehicle or person intrudes.
Measured nuisance-alarm prevalence supports context-aware handling rather than sensor improvement alone.
Berms are nuisance-warning examples in one fact, protective detections not nuisance in the other.
Volvo's slope-memory mechanism substantiates ordinary stockpiling work creating false-stop problems.
